While any kineticist can learn the rudiments of healing, some are virtuosos of the curative arts. The kinetic chirurgeon trades her entire shaping discipline - infusions, metakinesis, infusion specialization - for the healer's craft: her touch knits flesh with raw elemental force, and as she grows, her healing learns to mend what flesh alone cannot.

With a touch, she heals a willing living creature, restoring 1d6 hit points plus her Constitution modifier for every 2 kineticist levels she possesses. Each use requires her to accept 1 point of burn - gather power and any other effect that reduces burn applies as usual - and if she cannot accept the burn, the healing does not happen. Each use also cures one condition afflicting the target - the worst her training covers, from fatigued and shaken at 3rd level up through blinded, frightened and finally stunned at 9th. From 5th level her Metahealer training adds one extra healing die (two at 11th, three at 17th), and at 17th level the same use mends both the target and herself. This replaces infusions and infusion specialization.

At 13th level she learns to mend herself in an instant: as a swift action, she may use kinetic healer on herself, at the normal cost of 1 point of burn. This replaces metakinesis (empower, maximize and quicken).
At 5th level, her healing deepens: kinetic healer rolls one additional healing die. This becomes two additional dice at 11th level and three at 17th.
At 17th level, the same use of kinetic healer mends both her target and herself.

The storm never stops moving, and neither does she. The stormcaller is the wind given a rider: faster than any kineticist, throwing more bolts than any kineticist, each one carrying less of the storm than a full blast - until the storm fully accepts her. Her lightning is true lightning, the kind that does not care what demons are immune to. She trades her elemental defense and every chance at a second element for the sky's single-mindedness.

The wind is always at her back: her land speed increases by 10 feet. She also gains a swift version of every air-family kinetic blast she possesses (air, electric, blizzard, charged water, plasma, sandstorm, thunderstorm) - a free action usable once per round, with each blast's damage dice halved. And her electricity is the storm's own: it ignores electricity immunity and resistance (the ascendant element of the mythic spheres, hers from the first day). This replaces enveloping winds and the expanded element line.
At 5th level, the wind pushes harder: her land speed increases by another 10 feet (20 feet total).

At 8th level, as a swift action she may blink to the side of any creature within close range - friend or foe - riding the current between one heartbeat and the next. The step carries no attack; it is pure motion.
At 12th level, she slips between the wind's moments: she may use her swift blasts twice per round.
At 16th level, the storm accepts her completely. Her swift blasts no longer halve their damage dice, and she becomes immune to electricity - the storm does not strike its own.

A swift version of the kinetic blast: a free action that keeps the blast's full attack roll and typing, with every damage entry's dice halved - more casts, less storm in each. Usable once per round (twice with Riding the Current); the round's charge is spent when the bolt is loosed - it lands or breaks on the wind, the storm does not refund it.

Some oracles speak for the gods. She speaks for the wounded. Her power is the oldest bargain in scripture: let the blow fall on me. She may speak her vow over companions (Intercession, a swift action): while marked, half of the damage a companion takes is transferred to her, beyond armor and beyond resistance. At mythic rank 4 the vow widens to two companions at once. A fallen vow-carrier carries nothing. Only oracles can take this mythic ability.
Speak the vow over one ally within close range (never herself): the ally gains the Mark of the Vow. A swift action, usable at will. When the vow is spoken at its capacity, the oldest mark passes on.
Her body answers for yours: half of the damage you take is transferred to her, beyond armor and beyond resistance. If she falls, the vow carries nothing.

A planar oracle has an affinity with one of the Outer Planes. She is at home on the multiple planes of the Great Beyond, and can eventually become an outsider herself. At 1st level she chooses a plane (Heaven, Hell, the Abyss, or the Maelstrom), each bound to one energy: at 3rd level she gains resistance 10 to that energy (20 at 11th), and at 20th she becomes an extraplanar creature - immune to her plane's energy, with damage reduction 10/magic. Her pilgrim's road is written in bonus spells (protection from evil, see invisibility, protection from energy, freedom of movement, dismissal, chain lightning, banishment, mind blank, elemental swarm), gained at the planar slots. This replaces her 3rd- and 7th-level revelations and her final revelation.
Choose the Outer Plane of your affinity. This choice cannot be changed.
The archons' plane of law and good. Your attuned energy is electricity, the light of the Silver City.
The devils' plane of law and evil. Your attuned energy is fire, the endless pits of Asmodeus.
The demons' plane of chaos and evil. Your attuned energy is cold, the lightless depths of the Worldwound's masters.
The proteans' plane of pure chaos. Your attuned energy is acid, the dissolving storm at the center of the Great Beyond.
At 3rd level, you gain energy resistance 10 against your chosen plane's associated energy type. This replaces the 3rd-level revelation.
At 11th level, your energy resistance against your chosen plane's energy type increases to 20.

At 20th level, you become an extraplanar creature. You gain superficial physical characteristics appropriate to natives of your chosen plane, gain immunity to your associated energy type, and gain damage reduction 10/magic. Unlike other outsiders, you can still be brought back from the dead. This replaces your final revelation.

Her scripture is not canon. She copied from the wizard's book, and her god let her keep it - for a price. At every oracle level she copies one wizard spell of a level she can cast into her spells known, cast as oracle spells with her own magic. Every stolen page is apocrypha, and every page is paid for in years of her own life: each theft permanently costs her 2 maximum hit points, and the price can never be healed or bargained away - only paid. Twenty spells by 20th level is forty hit points of book. This replaces every revelation of her mystery (3rd, 7th, 11th, 15th, and 19th level).
Copy one wizard spell of a level you can cast into your oracle spells known. The theft is paid for in years of your own life: each stolen spell permanently reduces your maximum hit points by 2.
A pilgrim's spell of the planes beyond, gained through the planar oracle's attunement.
A spell copied from the wizard's book into her own - a page of apocrypha. The theft permanently costs 2 maximum hit points; the price is never refunded.

While paladins often are seen mounted atop a loyal steed, the shining knight is the true symbol of mounted bravery. She is never far from her steed, and hers is the charge that shatters morale: at 3rd level her mount shares her divine grace, at 5th her divine bond must be the steed, and at 11th a mounted charge that strikes her smitten quarry forces a Will save or panics it. This replaces divine health, the weapon option of divine bond, and aura of justice.

Any mount she rides shares her conviction: the mount gains the benefit of her divine grace, adding her Charisma bonus (if any) to its saving throws. (The tabletop's Ride-skill clause has no meaning in this world - there are no Ride checks - and is cut.) This replaces divine health.

Whenever her mounted charge hits the target of her smite evil, the target must make a Will save (DC 10 + half her paladin level + her Charisma modifier) or be panicked for a number of rounds equal to half her paladin level. (The tabletop's no-provoke clause has no engine here - the charge still draws attacks of opportunity - and is cut.) This replaces aura of justice.

She swore her oath not to a god of order but to chance itself - the open road, the roll of the die, the freedom of the unrepeated moment. Only the chaotic may walk her road. Fate's Wager rides every blow she strikes: on a natural 1-4 the attack scatters and misses outright, on a natural 17+ the dice surge and the hit deals an extra 1d6 per two paladin levels. She laughs at fear - a luck bonus on saves against fear equal to her Charisma modifier - but she is not immune to it, as a paladin of order would be. Her blade carries chaos: her physical damage counts as chaotic-aligned. She has no lay on hands, no mercies, no smite, and no channel - chance keeps what healing and vengeance would return - and her auras are not orders but luck: the Open Road, Whimsy, the Wandering Star, Fortune's Favor, and at last the Laughing Fool, which shares her wager with all who fight beside her. This replaces lay on hands, all mercies, smite evil, channel positive energy, and every aura of the base paladin.

Every weapon attack she makes rides the die. On a natural d20 roll of 1-4, the blow scatters - a miss even if her modifiers would hit. On a natural 17+, the dice surge: the hit deals an extra 1d6 of damage per two paladin levels. The surge stacks with critical hits. She also laughs at fear: a luck bonus on saves against fear equal to her Charisma modifier (minimum +2) - not the immunity of an ordered paladin. And her blade carries chaos: her physical damage counts as chaotic-aligned. Fortune is not fair, and neither is she.
Allies within 10 feet (herself included) gain a +1 luck bonus on attack rolls. This replaces aura of courage.
+1 luck bonus on attack rolls, carried on the fool's road.

Allies within 10 feet (herself included) gain damage reduction that grows with her: 2 at 8th level, 3 at 11th, 4 at 14th, and 5 at 17th, where it stops. No weapon, no magic, no material pierces it; only damage in excess of it. This replaces aura of resolve.
Damage reduction that grows with the Fool herself - no weapon pierces it, only damage in excess of it.

Allies within 10 feet (herself included) carry her lesser blessing: their weapon hits on a natural d20 roll of 17+ deal an extra 2d6 damage - but the star spends itself when it fires, and returns only with her next turn. This replaces aura of justice.
Your weapon hits on a natural d20 roll of 17+ deal an extra 2d6 damage. Once it fires, the star leaves you until her next turn.
Allies within 10 feet (herself included) gain a +2 luck bonus on all saving throws. This replaces aura of faith.
+2 luck bonus on all saving throws.

Her companions within 10 feet carry Fate's Wager itself: their weapon attacks scatter on a natural 1-4 and surge on a natural 17+ with an extra 1d6 per two of her paladin levels. She already carries the wager - it does not stack with itself. This replaces aura of righteousness.
Fate's Wager rides your blows: on a natural 1-4 your attack scatters and misses; on a natural 17+ it deals an extra 1d6 per two paladin levels.

Many rangers are loners, but the guide walks with others - and brings them home. He forgoes the favored enemy of his peers to focus on the task at hand: a swift mark upon one foe, luck spent on a single die, a moment of perfect clarity when it matters most. His camp is a moving school of woodcraft - quick to act, sharp of eye, soft of foot - and he gives it all away. This replaces favored enemy (all ranks), hunter's bond, evasion, improved evasion, quarry, and improved quarry; master hunter remains.

Once per day, plus one additional use per three levels after 1st, he can focus on a single enemy within line of sight as a swift action. The mark holds until the target dies or he names a new focus. He gains a +2 bonus on attack and damage rolls against his focus, increasing by +2 at 5th level and every five levels thereafter (+2, +4, +6, +8, +10). This replaces favored enemy.

Swift action: mark one enemy within line of sight as your focus. The mark holds until the target dies or you name a new focus. You gain a bonus on attack and damage rolls against your focus: +2, increasing by +2 at 5th level and every five levels thereafter.
The guide has named this creature his focus. He gains a bonus on attack and damage rolls against it - and he does not miss twice.

At 4th level, the guide forms a bond with the land itself and directs others through it: he and all allies within 30 feet gain a +2 bonus on initiative checks and on Perception, Stealth, and Lore (Nature) checks - Survival in the tabletop, the wilderness skill here. This replaces hunter's bond.
+2 on initiative, Perception, Stealth, and Lore (Nature). The guide's camp is a moving school of woodcraft.

At 9th level, once per day, as a swift action, the guide wraps his next attack of the round in luck: if that attack misses, the die rolls again. The second result stands. One additional use per day at 14th and 19th level. This replaces evasion.
Swift action: your next attack this round, if it misses, is rerolled. The second result stands - even if it is worse, though only a miss can summon the luck.
Your next attack roll this round that misses is rerolled. The luck spends itself when it fires.

At 11th level, once per day, as a free action, the guide can have an inspired moment: until the end of his next turn his speed increases by 10 feet, he gains a +4 bonus to AC and on attack rolls, and every critical threat he scores is automatically confirmed. Twice per day at 19th level. This replaces quarry and improved quarry.
Free action: for 1 round, +10 foot speed, +4 AC, +4 on attack rolls, and every critical threat is automatically confirmed.
+10 foot speed, +4 AC, +4 on attack rolls, and every critical threat is automatically confirmed. One clear moment, spent well.
At 16th level, his luck hardens: every reroll made with ranger's luck carries a +4 luck bonus on the attack roll. This replaces improved evasion.

Some rangers hunt a favored enemy; the wildbonded never needed one - they have a partner instead. Her animal companion answers from 1st level, and the bond between them shapes the beast itself: a bear that maules, a boar that will not die quietly, a dog that sets up every strike, an elk that stamps with a phantom herd, a leopard that marks the kill, a mastodon that breaks formations, a smilodon that finishes one thing at a time, a raptor that tears armor for its master, a wolf that makes the whole party a pack, a triceratops that becomes a wall. The price: no favored enemy, no favored terrain, no evasion - and no spells until 12th level. The beast is the spells.

Your animal companion carries a species bond that grows with you, improving at 4th, 8th, 12th, 16th, and 20th level. See the bond of your chosen beast. This replaces hunter's bond; the companion itself arrives at 1st level.

The bond deepens. Your companion's bond improves to its second tier: the bear's ward hardens, the boar's fury doubles, the dog runs farther, the phantom elk closes the gap, the leopard's precision grows, the mastodon needs less momentum, the smilodon's stacks climb higher, the raptor's rend deepens, the pack howls wider - and the pack gains attack speed.

The bond deepens again (third tier) - and your spells return, eight levels late. The bear wards harder, the boar heals more, the leopard strikes past concealment's edge (+2), the mastodon's impact widens, the smilodon earns an extra attack at six stacks, the raptor's rend bites 1d6, the pack reaches 30 feet at +2/-2.

The bond deepens (fourth tier): the boar frenzies at three quarters health, the phantom elk nearly matches the real one, the mastodon needs but two rounds of momentum, the pack howls every other round - and answers a wounded ally on its own.

The bond completes (fifth tier): the bear's ward is iron, the boar's frenzy is a storm, the phantom elk is the elk, the leopard's precision is 5d6, the smilodon hunts with twelve stacks of bloodshed, the raptor's rend is 1d8, the wolf answers any enemy that fights beside it - and the triceratops's second charge hits like the first.
The bond rides the beast: it grows with the ranger's level.
Mauled by the bear: -10 speed, and its blows against the bear's master land softer.
The bear is ready to answer its master's strike against a mauled enemy - once per round.
The boar's fury, boiled over: bonus damage on every strike, a second wind already spent, and fear forgotten.
The dog has marked this creature as its prey. When its master strikes the prey, the dog runs; when the dog has it down, the master strikes true.
Prone beneath the hound: the ranger gains a bonus on attack and damage rolls against this creature.
The master struck the prey - the dog gains +15 speed for a round.
Marked by the leopard. The ranger's attacks against this creature deal bonus precision damage.
The leopard watches for a vulnerable moment - once per round it can mark.
The mastodon is moving, and something is about to break.
Caught in the mastodon's impact: -10 speed.
The smilodon's consecutive strikes build: +1 damage per two stacks. Switch targets and it is lost.
Six stacks of bloodshed: the smilodon strikes with an extra attack each round while the streak holds.
The raptor's talons have done their work. The ranger's next attack consumes every stack.
The rending relay pays off: -2 AC for a round.
The wolf's howl rides you: bonuses against enemies adjacent to the wolf - and from the second tier, attack speed. Enemies beset by two of the pack suffer.
After its charge, the triceratops plants itself: bonus AC, unable to be tripped, and allies nearby gain +2 AC.
The bulwark is broken into momentum: +10 speed, and its next hit deals +2d6.
Riding the bond: +10 speed, and mounted charges hit harder as you grow together.
The centipede's venom, deepened by every strike of its master: -1 to all saves per rank.
The monitor's bite lingers - and the beast drinks the strength of it.
The wolf watches - once per round, an enemy that fights beside it answers to fang and master alike.
Swift action: command the triceratops to end its bulwark and ready a second charge (+10 speed; its next hit deals +2d6).

Swift action (the hound's): command the dog to designate one enemy as its Prey. When you strike the prey, the hound gains +15 speed for a round; while the prey is prone, you gain a bonus on attack and damage rolls against it. The hound keeps its prey until you command a new one.

Not all rogues live in the city. Scouts roam the wilderness - bandits, trailblazers, companions to rangers and barbarians - and they kill on the move. Her charge lands like an ambush, and a scout who has covered ground strikes as if from hiding. This replaces uncanny dodge and improved uncanny dodge; everything else about the rogue is untouched.

At 4th level, whenever the scout makes a charge, her attack treats the target as flat-footed - sneak attack damage lands, and the target's Dexterity bonus to AC is denied. Foes with uncanny dodge are immune to this ability. This replaces uncanny dodge.

At 8th level, whenever the scout moves more than 10 feet in a round and makes an attack, the attack treats the target as flat-footed - but only the first attack she makes that round. Foes with uncanny dodge are immune to this ability. This replaces improved uncanny dodge.

Some rogues knife from the shadows; this one rains steel from thirty feet away. Javelins, throwing axes, darts - her hands are always moving, and there is always another blade. Quick hands, a cruel ricochet, a wrist that lends Dexterity to every throw, and the knack of catching a blade that comes back clean and sending it out again. This replaces trapfinding and danger sense; sneak attack, evasion, uncanny dodge, rogue talents, debilitating injuries, and master strike are untouched - the knife was always the trade. This one simply flies.
At 1st level, she gains a +1 bonus on attack rolls with thrown weapons. The bonus increases to +2 at 8th level and +3 at 16th. This replaces trapfinding.
At 6th level, she adds her Dexterity modifier to damage rolls with thrown weapons, on top of the Strength the throw already carries. Her arm was always the point.

At 12th level, once per round, when she kills a creature with a thrown weapon, the blade comes back clean and goes out again: an immediate free attack at the nearest living enemy within 30 feet. On a hit, the returning throw deals 1d6 + her Dexterity modifier.
Her hands only know the throw. She takes a -2 penalty on attack rolls with any weapon that is not a thrown weapon - blades and bows alike. The price of the Steel Rain.

She does not fight enemies; she studies them - and every failure is a lesson. A miss against a target she could barely reach teaches her a seam in its armor, and she never forgets a seam; the harder the target, the faster she learns, and what she cannot learn she takes by force - trading her own guard for the opening. Strike a spellcaster and her study wards her from magic; strike an armored thing and she finds the joint. Given time she knows exactly where the knife goes. This replaces trapfinding and danger sense; sneak attack, evasion, uncanny dodge, rogue talents, debilitating injuries, and master strike are untouched.

At 1st level, whenever she misses with an attack that needed a high natural roll to hit, she finds a seam: a permanent, stacking +1 bonus on attack rolls against that enemy. The qualifying roll falls as she levels - 16 at 1st, dropping by 1 every three levels to 10 at 18th - so her study keeps pace with her sharpening aim. This replaces trapfinding.
The anatomist has found the seams in this creature's armor: a stacking +1 bonus on her attack rolls against it. She does not forget.

At 8th level, her study turns to how enemies defend themselves. Whenever she attacks a spellcaster, she gains spell resistance (4 + her rogue level) for 1 round. Whenever she damages an enemy that has damage reduction, she deals +1 additional damage per five rogue levels - the same reading, not stackable.
Her study of the caster's craft guards her: spell resistance 4 + her rogue level, for as long as she keeps attacking spellcasters.
At 16th level, once per round, when she hits an enemy carrying five or more of her seams, the strike is an automatic critical. She has known where the knife goes for a while now.

Swift action: she drops her guard (-6 AC for 1 round) to find an opening - her next attack this round applies a seam to its target whether it hits or misses. No roll needed; the opening is taken, not given. If she does not attack, the guard was simply spent.
Her guard is spent: -6 AC, and her next attack this round will find a seam whether it lands or not.

At 12th level, against enemies carrying her seams, she reads the telegraphs before they move: a +2 dodge bonus to AC against every one of them. The longer she has studied a thing, the less it can surprise her.

A witch of this bent does not keep a familiar. She keeps a beast, and the beast keeps what it kills.
The Chimera trades her familiar, eight of her ten hex levels (the first two hex grants are kept), and one spell slot per spell level at class levels 6 and above for an animal companion of legendary appetite. Whenever her companion slays a creature of a type it has not yet eaten, it takes a piece of the kill and grows a permanent trait from that creature's flesh - one course per creature type, twelve types in all.
Note: prestige classes that advance the witch spellbook (Mystic Theurge and the like) do not advance the Chimera's thinned spellbook.
Choose the beast the witch bonds with. It grows with her full class level and carries the chimera's diet: whatever it kills, it takes a piece of.

The witch's bond is not a familiar's whisper but a beast's hunger. When her companion kills a creature of a type it has not yet eaten, it takes a piece of the kill and grows a permanent trait from that flesh. Humanoids leave no piece worth taking, and the witch's own kills are hers, not the beast's.
Strange meat reshapes strange minds. The beast gains a +2 insight bonus on Will saves.
The beast has eaten aberration flesh and grown alien minds.
Kinship, devoured. The beast's speed increases by 10 feet.
The beast has eaten animal flesh and found it familiar.
Gears and plating settle in the gut. The beast gains damage reduction 2/adamantine.
The beast has eaten construct parts and digested stone.
Something old and precise wakes behind its eyes. The beast gains a +1 competence bonus on attack rolls.
The beast has eaten dragon flesh and dreams of hoards.
Caprice, swallowed whole. The beast gains a +2 insight bonus on Reflex saves.
The beast has eaten fey flesh and learned to laugh at danger.
The moon's mark, eaten. The beast gains damage reduction 2/silver.
The beast has eaten lycanthrope flesh and carries the moon's mark.
It eats another monster and wears it. The beast gains a +2 natural armor bonus to AC.
The beast has eaten magical beast flesh and wears the monster now.
Predator eats predator. The beast gains a +2 competence bonus on initiative checks.
The beast has eaten monstrous humanoid flesh and hunts first.
The blood of another world burns hot. The beast gains fire resistance 10.
The beast has eaten outsider flesh and its blood burns.
Green stubbornness, chewed and kept. The beast gains a +2 insight bonus on Fortitude saves.
The beast has eaten plant matter and grown patient roots.
Death itself, tasted. The beast gains a +1 insight bonus on all saving throws.
The beast has eaten undead flesh and been greeted by the grave.
A thousand small lessons in escape. The beast becomes immune to the entangled condition.
The beast has eaten vermin and knows how small things slip free.

Among witches, there are those who devote themselves to the care of others and restrict their practices to the healing arts. They often take the place of clerics in rural communities, wandering the countryside and tending to the sick.
The hedge witch trades the hexes she would learn at 4th and 8th level for the healer's true arts: her prepared spells can be channeled into healing, and she can draw poison and disease out of the afflicted - taking their pain into herself.

The hedge witch can channel stored spell energy into healing spells she did not prepare ahead of time. She can 'lose' any prepared spell that is not a cantrip in order to cast any cure spell of the same spell level or lower - from cure light wounds to mass heal - even if she does not know that cure spell.
(Regenerate is not in the game; 7th-level slots convert to heal instead, which the same-or-lower rule allows.)

As a standard action, the hedge witch can minister to a diseased or poisoned creature with a touch, drawing the affliction out of them entirely - all poisons and diseases are removed.
The witch suffers the remembered pain: she immediately takes 2d6 points of damage as the last echoes of the affliction pass through her.
(Tabletop port: the original redirects the victim's next failed save to the witch; Wrath does not expose affliction internals, so the port cures outright and charges a fixed pain instead.)
The hedge witch has drawn an affliction out of someone else; its last echo hurts her still.

Considered bringers of fortune and prosperity, a jiuweihu is a kitsune shaman who has been blessed with multiple tails by the spirits of unseen kami. In rare cases, evil jiuweihu who are instead championed by wicked oni are created.
The jiuweihu trades her spirit animal for a star jewel - the spirit rests in a grape-sized gem that cannot be slain - and grows a new magical tail at 1st level and every two levels thereafter, each granting a spell-like ability. Only kitsune may take this archetype.
(Tabletop port note: the game embeds shaman spirit magic inside each spirit, so the tabletop's spirit-magic trade could not be excised - the jiuweihu keeps her spirit magic, and the port is up one trade as a result.)

The jiuweihu's spirit does not prowl at her side - it rests in a star-cut gem the size of a grape, warm to the touch and quietly alive. The jewel cannot be slain, charmed, or frightened, and needs no feeding.
As a bringer of fortune, the jiuweihu gains a +1 luck bonus on all saving throws.
(Tabletop port: the original jewel bound hex lets the familiar transform into an item - orbit like an ioun stone, gain hardness, and so on. The game has no item-form familiars, so the spirit simply stays in the jewel and grants its fortune.)

The ninth tail is the one the myths agree on: it belongs to the spirit, not the fox. Choose one of your Magical Tail spell-like abilities; you can use it one additional time per day. You cannot choose the same tail twice.

Something else wears her face now. The Spirit-Ridden did not bargain with the spirits - she lost the argument, and they moved in.
Almost nothing of the shaman remains: no spells, no hexes, no spirit animal, not even her spirit. In exchange, the heroes of dead ages inhabit her body - and she can let one of them take the reins at will.
At 1st, 6th, 12th and 18th level she invites another spirit in (two answer the first call, two more come at 6th, one at 12th, one at 18th). Channeling a spirit is a swift action and lasts until she switches or expels it. While a spirit holds the reins she takes on its role - fighting as a fighter, barbarian, monk, rogue, ranger or paladin of her shaman level minus two (the first two levels suffer no reduction).
The spirit also dresses its vessel: while she is wearing NOTHING, the spirit's arms and armor manifest - a level-appropriate enhancement to attack, damage and armor class. Wear anything of your own and the spirit's regalia refuses to appear.

Choose a spirit of a dead hero to inhabit the shaman's body. Each spirit is a form she can channel at will as a swift action: while channeled, she fights as that spirit's class at her shaman level minus two (no reduction for the first two levels), and - if her body is bare - the spirit's equipment manifests on her. Only one spirit can hold the reins at a time.
The Weapon Saint and the Red Warlord answer a first call; the Barefoot Master and the Cutthroat come at 6th level, the Grey Hunter at 12th, and the First Knight at 18th.

A swordsman who died mid-perfect-cut and never accepted it. While the Saint holds the reins she fights as a FIGHTER: all armor and shield proficiencies, a fighter's full attack progression, and a growing edge on attack and damage rolls (+1 per four effective levels).

A warlord whose last battle never ended. While the Warlord holds the reins she fights as a BARBARIAN: martial weapons, a barbarian's full attack progression, and the warlord's unquiet fury - Strength and Constitution surge by +2, rising to +4 and +6 as she grows, Will saves rise by +2, and her recklessness costs her 2 points of armor class.

An ascetic who forgot to stop walking. While the Master holds the reins she fights as a MONK: the monk's weapon arts, a slowly climbing dodge bonus to armor class (+1 per four effective levels), and the Master's impossible stride (+20 feet of speed).

A killer whose blade still wants work. While the Cutthroat holds the reins she fights as a ROGUE: the first wound she lands each round runs deeper, dealing an extra 1d6 damage per three effective levels, and her eye for the opening sharpens (+2 initiative).

A tracker who follows prey into death itself. While the Hunter holds the reins she fights as a RANGER: martial weapons, a ranger's full attack progression, a growing eye for the kill (+1 attack per four effective levels), and the Hunter's tireless pace (+10 feet of speed).

A paladin who fell at the Worldwound's first opening - and simply refused to stop guarding it. While the Knight holds the reins she fights as a PALADIN: heavy armor and shields, a paladin's full attack progression, climbing dodge and resistance bonuses to defense (+1 per four and per three effective levels), and the Knight's fearlessness: immunity to shaken and frightened.

A druid of the old forests who poured herself into the roots rather than let her grove burn - and never fully died. While the Antlered One holds the reins, a dire wolf of the old forest answers her call: it appears beside the vessel and fights for as long as the spirit stays, fading the moment she withdraws. The vessel keeps the druid's lesser arts: the Thorn Lash and the Mend.
A whip of living thorns rakes a single target: 1d6 piercing damage per two shaman levels (maximum 10d6). Reflex halves.
Roots and sap knit torn flesh: heals the target 1d6 damage per two shaman levels (maximum 10d6).

A sorceress who chose to burn rather than surrender her city, and whose fire never went out. While the Pyre Empress holds the reins, the vessel wields her fire - the Cinder Bolt and the Pyre Burst - as often as she can bear to raise her hand.
A lance of the Empress's fire strikes a single target: 1d6 fire damage per two shaman levels (maximum 10d6). Reflex halves.
The fire that took her city, briefly relit: a 20-foot burst of flame dealing 1d6 fire damage per two shaman levels (maximum 10d6) to enemies in the area. Reflex halves.

A wizard who catalogued every death in the Worldwound, and read the ledger so often that the fears learned to read back. While the Pale Archivist holds the reins, the vessel speaks her indices of dread. (She teaches no wards and no blessings - a spirit that lent its strength before a battle would be worth more than the vessel herself, so the ledger holds only fears.)
The Archivist reads a single target its own entry: Will save or become frightened for 2 rounds.
The ledger falls open and the page stares back: enemies within 30 feet must pass a Will save or be shaken for 2 rounds.

A duelist who fused sword and spell so thoroughly that neither survived her apart. While the Spellblade holds the reins, the vessel fights with the magus's weapon arts, and every weapon strike carries her parting fire: +1d6 fire damage per five effective levels.

The spell warrior uses his arcane knowledge rather than his rage to turn the tide of battle in favor of himself and his allies. With a clash of bracers and a sonorous chant, his song reaches out to touch the weapons of his allies, lending them arcane power. While his song does not inspire rage, he can use the power of his music to enchant the weapons of his allies. (The counterspelling arts of the tabletop warrior have no place in the Worldwound's wars - this port carries the weapon song only.)

A raging song of a different kind: while it plays, the weapons of all allies within 60 feet gain an enhancement bonus - +1 at 1st level, increasing by 1 at 5th level and every 5 levels thereafter (to a maximum of +5 at 20th). The bonus overlaps (does not stack with) any enhancement a weapon already has, and the song drains raging-song rounds for every round it plays.
The spell warrior's song flows through allied steel: weapons wielded by allies within 60 feet are enchanted while the song plays.

Not rage but rhythm. The crescendo skald's song does not throw allies into a fury - it picks them up and carries them, building speed as each of them finds their mark. Allies who keep landing blows and spells rise with the music; one quiet round and that momentum is spent. Spellcasting is never blocked: momentum flows through sword and spell alike. (A MissionWOTR homebrew.)

A raging song of momentum rather than fury. While it plays, every ally within 60 feet builds Momentum: one stack each round in which they land at least one attack or complete at least one spell (maximum 5 stacks). A round in which an ally lands nothing resets that ally's Momentum to zero - only that ally's. Momentum grants morale bonuses to Strength and Constitution (+1 at one stack, +2 at three, +3 at five) and +1 on Will saves, at a cost of 1 AC while it lasts. The song drains one raging-song round per round and ends when none remain.

The crescendo carries this ally: a morale bonus to Strength and Constitution (+1 at one stack of Momentum, +2 at three, +3 at five) and +1 on Will saves, at a cost of 1 AC while it lasts. Each round with at least one landed attack or completed spell adds a stack (maximum 5); a round with nothing landed resets it - and only this ally's.

A slayer who hunts the mind, not the blind side. The Dreadnaught wears the heaviest plate without caring who sees her coming, and her study breaks a foe's resolve instead of guiding blades to its vitals: the mark she lays drains courage, will, and luck from every saving throw. She trades every ounce of sneak attack and one talent for armor that does not hide her, a will that does not break, and a presence that empties enemies before a blade is drawn. (A MissionWOTR homebrew.)

A swift-action study that MARKS a foe: a penalty on all of its saving throws (-1 at 1st level, increasing by 1 at 5th and every 5 levels thereafter, to -5 at 20th) for ten minutes. There is no attack or damage bonus - her study breaks resolve, not guard. A fresh mark also attempts to demoralize the foe: a Persuasion check against 10 + its level + its Wisdom; on a success it is shaken for 1 minute. She adds half her level (minimum 1) on Persuasion checks and is proficient with heavy armor.
The Dreadnaught's mark: a penalty on all three saving throws while it lasts. The deeper her study, the deeper the dread.
The Dreadnaught's Will is not the slayer's weak one, but stands halfway to a champion's: +1 at 1st level, +2 at 8th, +3 at 15th.

While paladins and inquisitors use their connection with the divine to fight undead hordes and other horrors of the night, a grave warden relies on knowledge, skill with weapons, and tenacity to put an end to these night-born terrors. His blade carries holy water's bite, he wards himself against death itself, and the oldest undead fear his finishing stroke: one that does not merely slay them, but unmakes them.

As a swift action, the grave warden anoints his held weapon for 1 round. While the anointment lasts, his weapon damage against undead creatures carries an additional 2d6 points of holy damage, as if from a direct hit by holy water.
As a standard action, the grave warden performs the warding rites upon himself, gaining the benefits of death ward for 1 minute per slayer level.

As a swift action, the grave warden marks a single undead creature for 1 round. If his next attack against it hits, the mark resolves: the target must succeed at a Will save (DC 10 + half his slayer level + his Intelligence modifier) or be destroyed outright. A target that saves is immune to this grave warden's dustbringer for 24 hours.
The grave warden's killing stroke waits upon the next blow that lands. When it does, the undead must save or be unmade.
This creature has withstood the grave warden's dustbringer within the last day and cannot be marked again yet.

An eldritch scrapper is usually spoiling for a fight, looking to prove that she's just as tough as a martial character. A veteran of many brawls against opponents who were suspicious of her manifesting magic, an eldritch scrapper has a thick skin and a fighting style that blends weapons with spells. She trains with every weapon a soldier might carry, and her battlefield instincts let her pick up combat tricks her caster studies never left time for. (Adapted port: the conflicting blood of the tabletop's trades is paid in spells known instead - one fewer at every level, the same price the crossblooded pays.)

Some sorcerers let the blood carry them. The overchanneler carries the blood: she opens the channel wider than her body was meant to bear, and every spell she throws through the open channel burns her as it leaves. In exchange, her magic strikes harder, lasts longer, and counts for more while the channel is open. She gives up a little endurance - one spell slot of every level per day - for peaks no careful caster will ever reach. (A MissionWOTR homebrew.)

As a swift action, the overchanneler opens the channel for 1 round: while it is open, her caster level is increased (+2 at 1st, +4 at 9th, +6 at 17th) and every spell she casts deals bonus damage equal to that bonus times the spell's level. The moment a spell leaves her through the open channel, her blood pays for it: she takes damage equal to 1d6 per level of the spell cast.
The channel is open: her caster level is increased and every spell she casts deals bonus damage equal to that bonus times the spell's level - and burns her for 3 damage per spell level as it leaves.
The channel is opened to its apex: +8 caster level, +8 damage per spell level, and no blood price. This peak can be reached once per day.
The overchanneler's veins have learned to close around the burn: her backlash damage can no longer reduce her below 1 hit point.
Once per day, the overchanneler may open the channel to its apex: +8 caster level and +8 damage per spell level for one round, with no backlash at all.
